tldr: The paper introduces MindAgent, an infrastructure for evaluating emergent multi-agent planning and coordination capabilities of LLMs, along with CUISINEWORLD—a virtual kitchen benchmark where LLMs coordinate multiple agents to complete dish orders.
contributions: Establishment of CUISINEWORLD, a new gaming scenario and benchmark based on a multi-agent virtual kitchen environment with 10 location types, 27 ingredient types, and 33 unique dishes across 12 levels.
Introduction of MindAgent, an infrastructure for interactive multi-agent planning with LLMs using in-context learning, few-shot demonstrations, planning rationals, and environmental feedback.
Extensive evaluations with multiple LLMs (GPT-4, Claude, LLaMA) demonstrating generalist multi-agent planner potential.
Deployment into real-world gaming scenarios including a customized VR version of CUISINEWORLD and adaptation to Minecraft.
methods: The authors designed CUISINEWORLD as a text-based virtual kitchen game formulated as an MDP, where a centralized LLM dispatcher issues scheduling commands (goto, get, put, activate, noop) to N agents to complete dish orders before they expire. They introduced a Collaboration Score (CoS) metric measuring average task completion rate across different task-interval conditions. MindAgent leverages in-context learning with prompt components including recipes, instructions, inference knowledge, one-shot demos, current state observations, and memory history, with action extraction via regex and validation via look-ahead checking.
results: Zero-shot multi-agent planning: powerful pretrained LLMs like GPT-4 can schedule 2-4 agents to complete dishes and collaborate with human players using only simple game instructions. In-context learning with few-shot demonstrations, Chain-of-Thought rationals, and on-the-fly feedback significantly boosted planning performance. LLMs showed strong generalization from fewer-agent to more-agent coordination and adaptation to new domains like Minecraft.
limitations: Multi-agent planning with LLMs is bottlenecked by challenging computation cost, context length limitation, and non-optimal plans. Full interaction history cannot fit into context windows, requiring selection of a fixed horizon. The problem is NP-hard (cannot be solved in polynomial time), and the centralized planning approach may not scale indefinitely.
